1359.title: Colors of the year
1359.howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and other churches that keep the church calendar change the colors of altar cloths and clergy vestments with the seasons, often purple for Advent and Lent, white for Christmas and Easter, red for Pentecost and green for ordinary time; Orthodox churches have their own color customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bells: they call to prayer, toll for the dead, and ring out for joy. Your line was for whom it tolls.

In the back room of a church there's a cupboard full of cloth. Purple, folded on one shelf. White and gold on another. A bright red. A tall stack of green. One week, someone takes the green cloth off the altar and the pulpit, folds it away, and hangs up purple. The minister's stole changes to match. Nobody makes an announcement. But someone who comes every week can glance at the front and know, without a calendar, what time of year it is. Today: colors of the year.

Churches that keep the church calendar mark its seasons with colors, on the altar, the pulpit, and what the clergy wear. Customs vary, and Orthodox churches have color customs of their own, but a pattern you may meet runs like this. First, purple: Advent, the weeks of waiting before Christmas, and Lent, the weeks of turning back before Easter. Purple is a king's color, and the Gospels give it a hard edge: before the crucifixion, Mark says, the soldiers "clothed him with purple," and mocked him as a king. So some readers hear in purple both waiting for a king and sorrow over what was done to one. Some churches use blue in Advent instead. Next, white, for Christmas and Easter. At the empty tomb, Mark says the women "saw a young man sitting on the right side, clothed in a long white garment." White for the feasts, for joy, for light. Then red, for Pentecost, when the Spirit came on the disciples: "And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." Red is fire, and some churches use it on the days that remember martyrs too. Last, green, for the long stretches between the big feasts, which some churches call ordinary time: the green season of day one hundred twenty. Green is growth, plain and slow. Ecclesiastes gives the whole cupboard its reason: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." In these churches, the year isn't one long gray line.

Find something in the color of the church season, a scarf, a ribbon, a leaf, or, if you don't know the season, something green, the color of the ordinary stretches. Let it stand for the season you yourself are in: waiting, celebrating, on fire, or just growing slowly. If you pray, you can say the line from Ecclesiastes: to every thing there is a season.
screen: `TO EVERY THING THERE IS A SEASON.`

Your line: time has colors. Each season, its own. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.

1360.title: Incense
1360.hook: let my prayer rise like incense (Psalm 141:2)
1360.howItsDone: In Orthodox and Catholic worship, and in some Anglican and Lutheran churches, a priest or deacon swings a censer toward the altar, the icons or the gospel book, and the people; other churches pray without incense.

segments.voice: Yesterday, colors of the year: purple, white, red and green, a calendar you can see. Your line was time has colors.

The smell arrives first. Sweet and sharp, resin and wood smoke, reaching the back of the church before the procession does. Then the sound: a small chain clinking. A priest comes up the aisle swinging a metal censer, and with every swing a gray ribbon of smoke curls out, hangs in the light from a high window, and slowly climbs. He turns and swings it toward the icons, toward the altar, and then toward the people, who bow as it passes. By the end of the service the smoke has drifted up into the roof, and the smell is in everyone's coats. Today: incense.

Incense is a part of worship you can watch going up, and more than one passage ties that rising smoke to prayer. Start with the psalm: "Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice." The psalmist wants their prayer to do what the smoke does: rise, and be noticed. Next, the temple. At the start of Luke's Gospel, a priest named Zechariah is chosen by lot to go into the temple and burn incense, and Luke adds a detail: "And the whole multitude of the people were praying without at the time of incense." Inside, smoke. Outside, prayer. The same hour, as if they were one act. Then, a gift. When the wise men find the child Jesus, they open their treasures: "gold, and frankincense, and myrrh." Frankincense is incense, brought by travelers from the east to be given away. Last, heaven itself. In Revelation, an angel stands at the altar with a golden censer, "And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand." In that picture, the prayers rise all the way to God. Orthodox and Catholic Christians use incense in worship, and so do some Anglican and Lutheran churches. Other Christians pray without it, and keep the psalm's thought without the smoke. In the psalm's picture, a prayer isn't meant to stay on the ground.
screen: `LET MY PRAYER BE SET FORTH AS INCENSE.`

segments.voice: If you have incense and it's safe to light, light it and watch the smoke climb; if not, open a jar from the kitchen, cinnamon, cloves, a bay leaf, and breathe it in slowly. Let the scent fill one breath, then another, and picture your breath rising. If you pray, you can say the psalm, let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense, or simply follow the scent.
screen: `LET MY PRAYER BE SET FORTH BEFORE THEE AS INCENSE.`

1361.title: Candles
1361.hook: a candle as a prayer that keeps burning when you leave
1361.howItsDone: In Orthodox and Catholic churches people light small candles before icons and statues for the living and the dead and leave them burning; other churches light candles on an Advent wreath or hold them at candlelight services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, incense: smoke that rises the way a prayer hopes to. Your line was prayer rises.

Near the side wall of a church, a stand of small candles. Some burning, some burned down to wax, some new. A man comes in on his lunch break, still in his work jacket. He drops a coin in the box, takes a fresh candle, lights it from one already burning, and sets it in its place. He stands a moment. Then he checks the time and goes back out into the noise. The candle doesn't go with him. It keeps burning in the quiet church, for whoever he lit it for, after he's back at his desk. Today: candles.

For the people who light one, a candle in church does something a spoken prayer can't: it keeps going when they stop. Start with light itself: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." In the psalm, light lets you take the next step. And Jesus says, as on day one hundred seventy-three, that a light is meant to be seen: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house." A candle on a stand is that sentence, burning. Next, a fire that stays lit. In Leviticus, the priests are told: "The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out." Then, prayer that doesn't stop. Paul tells the church in Thessalonica, "Pray without ceasing." So some Christians, Orthodox and Catholic among them, light a candle before an icon or a statue, for someone who is sick, someone far away, someone who has died, and say that the flame goes on praying after they've walked out the door. Other churches light candles in their own ways, on an Advent wreath or held in the hand on Christmas Eve. Last, the person. Proverbs goes further: "The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD." In that picture, a candle isn't only something a person lights. A person is one. So the small flame on the stand is lit by someone, for someone.
screen: `THE SPIRIT OF MAN IS THE CANDLE OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it where you can see it; if not, turn on a small lamp or any light near you. Bring one person to mind, someone you love, someone struggling, someone you miss, and let the flame stand for them. If you pray, hold them in your prayer while you watch it; if you don't, keep them in mind, as steady as the flame.
Candles. Small flames lit in churches for someone, living or dead, so a prayer can go on burning after whoever lit it has gone.
Your line: a prayer left burning. It stays lit when you go. See you tomorrow.

1362.title: Cross and crucifix
1362.hook: an empty cross, or Christ on it: churches choose differently
1362.howItsDone: Catholic churches keep a crucifix on or near the altar, Orthodox churches often use crosses with Christ painted on them, and Protestant churches often display a plain cross; Christians of every kind may wear either on a chain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, candles: a small flame that keeps going after you've walked out the door. Your line was a prayer left burning.

On a jeweler's tray, two silver necklaces, same chain, same shape. One is a plain cross: two bars, nothing else. The other carries a tiny figure, arms stretched wide, head bowed. In one church, the big cross above the altar has that figure on it. Across the street, the cross on the wall is bare wood. Nobody in either building forgot anything. Each one chose. And the two choices say the same sentence, with the stress on different words.
screen: `ONE CHURCH: A FIGURE. ONE CHURCH: BARE WOOD.`

segments.voice: Day eighteen asked why an execution became the sign on the steeple. Today, two ways of showing it. First, the plain difference. A crucifix is a cross with the figure of Christ on it; a cross on its own has nobody on it. Both point at the same death, an execution the letter to the Hebrews places outside the city gate. That's the strange thing: an instrument of death ended up on necklaces and steeples. Paul wrote to the Galatians: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Next, the crucifix. Catholic churches keep one on or near the altar, and Orthodox Christians often use crosses with Christ painted on them, like an icon. Paul told the church in Corinth: "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." Some who pray before a crucifix say it keeps the cost in view: a real body, real nails, nothing tidied away. Then the empty cross. In other churches, Protestant ones especially, the cross is bare. To those who choose it, the emptiness is the message. In Matthew, the women come to the tomb at dawn, and the angel says: "He is not here: for he is risen, as he said." The bare cross points to that morning. Last, side by side. Churches with a crucifix still sing about the empty tomb; churches with a bare cross still read the story of the nails. One story: one holds the death in view, the other the morning after. In both, the whole sentence gets said: he died, and he rose.
screen: `AN INSTRUMENT OF DEATH, WORN ON A CHAIN.`
`THE BARE CROSS: HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Look at a cross, a necklace, a picture, a steeple out the window, or the one on the screen, and notice first whether it's empty or carries a figure. Let your eyes move slowly along the upright beam, the crossbeam, the place where the two meet. If you pray, you can pray in the words your own church uses before a cross; if you don't, simply look, and let it be a shape that carries a story.
Cross and crucifix. The bare shape, and the shape with Christ on it: two ways of showing one story.
Your line: he died, he rose. Two shapes, one sentence. Until tomorrow.

1363.title: Writing icons
1363.hook: iconographers pray and fast as they paint
1363.howItsDone: In Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches, iconographers traditionally pray before and during their work, may keep a fast, and follow patterns handed down for each saint; the finished icons are blessed and placed in churches and homes for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cross and crucifix: one holds the death in view, the other the morning after. Your line was he died, he rose.

A small room, early morning. A wooden board, coated smooth and white. Beside it, jars of colored powder, an egg, a cup of water, brushes. The painter hasn't eaten breakfast, and won't until the day's work is done. Before touching a brush, they stand, make the sign of the cross, and pray. Then they begin, not with a blank idea, but with a pattern handed down for this exact face. One line, then another. The finished face will hang in a church or a home, with candles lit before it. Orthodox Christians have a particular word for this. They don't always call it painting.
screen: `A WHITE BOARD, AN EGG, A CUP OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Some Orthodox Christians speak of writing an icon rather than painting one, because an icon is read, like a page. Its faces, hands, colors and gestures follow patterns passed down from earlier icons, so the iconographer isn't inventing a new look for a saint. They're copying a text faithfully, the way a scribe copies a Gospel: handing something on, not showing off a style. Next, the prayer. Tradition says the iconographer prays before and during the work, and some keep a fast. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his listeners to fast quietly, not for show. An icon is made in that spirit, traditionally without a signature: the hand at work, the heart turned toward God. Then, why pictures at all. Back in year three, the icon wars turned on this. Orthodox Christians point to John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Once God has a human face, that face can be painted. Some Protestant churches keep their walls bare, reading the commandment in Exodus: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image." Each side takes that text seriously, and reads it differently. Last, the craftsman. In Exodus, God names an artisan, Bezalel: "I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." Skill with the hands, counted as a gift of the spirit. Iconographers stand in that line.
screen: `AN ICON IS READ, LIKE A PAGE.`

segments.voice: With a pen and any scrap of paper, draw one simple thing in front of you, a cup, a leaf, your own hand, so slowly that each line takes a full breath, with no erasing and no judging. The point is attention, not a good drawing. If you pray, you can pray before the first line, the way an iconographer does; if you don't, let the slowness itself be the practice.
Writing icons. Making a holy image in prayer and fasting, following patterns handed down, so it can be read like a page.
Your line: painting as prayer. The hand at work, the heart turned toward God. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1364.title: Hymnals
1364.hook: the book in the pew held a people's theology
1364.howItsDone: In Protestant and Catholic churches a hymnal often sits in the pews and the congregation sings from it together; Orthodox churches sing hymns from their service books, and some newer churches project the words on a screen instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, writing icons: a holy face made in prayer, by a pattern handed down. Your line was painting as prayer.

The pew in front of you has a slot cut into its back. In it, a thick book with a cracked spine and a faded cloth cover. Somebody's pencil has marked a page; a funeral program is tucked in at another. Every page has lines of music above the words. Nobody would call it a theology book. It has no arguments, no footnotes. And yet a grandmother who never read a word of theology can sing half of it from memory, and in those songs is much of what her church believes about God, sin, grace and heaven.
screen: `A SLOT IN THE BACK OF THE PEW.`

segments.voice: Start with the Gospels. After the last supper, Matthew says, "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." Jesus's last evening with his friends ends with a song. In Acts, Paul and Silas sit in prison, feet in the stocks: "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." Next, why sing at all. Paul writes to the Colossians: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." Singing sits under teaching. A hymn is a lesson that gets into your memory through the back door. Then, the book. A hymnal gathers what a church wants its people to carry, so it tells you what that church holds dear. Martin Luther's hymn, in one old English version, opens: "A mighty fortress is our God, a bulwark never failing." A whole teaching about trust, in one line you can sing on the way home. Not every church uses a hymnal. Orthodox churches sing hymns from their service books, and some newer churches put the words up on a screen. The habit underneath is the same. Last, Isaac Watts, whom you met back on day one hundred thirty-six: "When I survey the wondrous cross, on which the Prince of glory died." The Prince of glory, dying: a whole doctrine about who was on the cross, sung without a footnote. That's the hymnal's quiet job.
screen: `THEY SANG A HYMN, AND WENT OUT.`

segments.voice: Read the verse on the screen, or a hymn you love, slowly, the way you'd read a letter. Then read it again, asking of each line: what does this say about God? If you pray, you can let the last line be your prayer; if you don't, notice which line you'd remember tomorrow, and why.
screen: `WHEN I SURVEY THE WONDROUS CROSS, ON WHICH THE PRINCE OF GLORY DIED, MY RICHEST GAIN I COUNT BUT LOSS, AND POUR CONTEMPT ON ALL MY PRIDE.`

segments.voice: Hymnals. The book of a church's songs, and of what it believes, carried in memory more than on a shelf.
Your line: theology in song. What a church sings, its people tend to carry home. Until tomorrow.

1365.title: Organs, guitars and drums
1365.howItsDone: Christians worship with pipe organs, pianos, guitars, drums and bands, or with no instruments at all: Orthodox churches and some Protestant churches, such as the Churches of Christ, sing unaccompanied.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymnals: what a church believes, carried home in song. Your line was theology in song.

The first note comes up through the floor before it reaches your ears: a low hum in your shoes, then a stone room filled with sound from a wall of metal pipes. Across town, a drummer clicks his sticks, one, two, three, four, and a guitar and a bass come in under a screen of lyrics. In a third church, there's no instrument at all. A single voice sings a line, and the room answers it. Ask in any of those rooms what's going on, and you may hear the same answer: praising God with what they have.

Start at the end of the Psalms. Psalm one hundred fifty is a list of instruments, and the King James Bible says: "Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs." Organs, right there. But some readers take the Hebrew word behind it as a simple pipe, nothing like a cathedral organ with pedals. The psalm was gathering every sound it knew. Next, the new. Another psalm says: "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise." Churches with guitars, drums and keyboards often point to lines like that. So do churches with pipe organs, which were once new themselves. Each generation brings the instruments it has. Then, the churches that use none. Orthodox churches traditionally sing their services without instruments, and so do some Protestant churches, such as the Churches of Christ. They read Paul's words to the Ephesians: "singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." For them, the human voice is the instrument God made. Each of these churches has reasons, and takes them seriously. Last, the end of that list psalm. After trumpet, harp, strings, pipes and two kinds of cymbal, it doesn't end on an instrument: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Every instrument on the list depends on breath, and every person has it.

Play a recording of an organ, a gospel band or a hymn with guitar, and listen for two minutes, noticing where the sound sits in your body: chest, feet, throat. If you can't play anything, listen to your own breathing, the instrument the psalm ends on. If you pray, you can let the music carry your prayer without words; if you don't, just listen all the way to the end.
Organs. The pipes in old churches, a word the King James Psalms already used, and a reminder that churches praise with the sounds they have.
Your line: every instrument praise. The week ran from colors of the year, incense and candles to the cross, icons, hymnals and organs: faith you can see, smell and hear. That's the week.

chat.says: My church has a band and drums. Is that less holy than an organ?
options: Churches differ, but Psalm 150 gathers every sound it knows and ends with all that has breath.
Yes; the Bible names only the pipe organ, so it's the one instrument meant for worship.
Instruments don't matter at all, since the Psalms never mention any of them by name.
chat.meaning: Psalm 150 lists instrument after instrument, then ends: let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Churches choose differently, each with reasons.
